sentences: A jade-green maebyeong, a classic Goryeo vase form, stands before us, 42.
1 centimetres tall.
It swells generously at the shoulder and narrows elegantly at the waist, and its whole surface is filled with cranes flying through clouds.
A maebyeong is a vessel with a small mouth, broad shoulders and a slim lower body.
This one was made in the Goryeo dynasty, around the thirteenth century.
It was designated a National Treasure in 1962 and belongs to the Kansong Art Museum.
Let's start at the top.
A neat little band rings the tiny mouth, and below it the shoulder rounds outward.
The S-curve flowing from shoulder to waist gives the vessel both tension and grace.
Look inside one of the circles drawn with a double line of black and white.
The crane within rises upward through the clouds, its white wings spread wide against the green ground, while its beak and legs are drawn in fine black lines.
Now look outside the circles.
These cranes seem to be descending.
So each time the vessel turns, the birds rise and fall around it, and the whole sky seems to move.
There are said to be sixty-nine cranes in all.
Because they fly in opposite directions, they seem far more numerous.
Since ancient times, the crane has been an auspicious bird, a symbol of long life, and together with clouds it evoked the realm of the immortals.
None of this is painted.
The potter carved the design into the clay, filled the grooves with white and red-brown slip, and fired it again.
In the kiln the red clay turns black, giving these black-and-white lines.
This inlay technique, perfected by Goryeo potters, is the great achievement of Korean celadon.
It gives the motifs a depth that seems to float up beneath the jade-green glaze.
Light passes through the glaze and softly lifts the lines set in the clay, so the pattern looks as if it lies under water.
Near the foot, a band of petal-like shapes wraps around the base.
The wide, flaring bottom firmly supports the body as it rises.
It has a calmer rhythm than the cranes and clouds above.
The vase was saved just before it could leave Korea.
In 1935 the collector Jeon Hyeong-pil paid a Japanese antiques dealer 20,000 won for it, a sum said to equal the price of twenty tiled houses at the time.
Step back and imagine turning this vase slowly in your hands.
Cranes rising inside the circles, cranes descending outside them: which ones does your eye follow first?
